title: Navigating Global Investments: RBI Limits, UCITS ETFs & Beyond
description: Indian investors are increasingly looking to diversify their portfolios globally beyond domestic options. The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) Liberalised Remitt.

faq.q: What is the RBI LRS limit for global investments?
faq.a: The RBI's Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) allows resident individuals to remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year for various purposes, including direct global investments. This is a cumulative limit across all remittances.

faq.q: Why did Indian mutual funds stop accepting money for international funds?
faq.a: Indian mutual funds paused fresh inflows into their international feeder funds because they were nearing or had hit the aggregate overseas investment limits (USD 7 billion + USD 1 billion for ETFs) set by SEBI for all AMCs combined.

faq.q: What are UCITS ETFs and how do they benefit Indian investors?
faq.a: UCITS ETFs are investment funds regulated under strict EU guidelines, offering diversification, transparency, and often lower costs. For Indian investors, they provide a regulated and accessible way to invest directly in global markets, especially given the restrictions on Indian international mutual funds.

faq.q: How are global investment gains taxed in India?
faq.a: Short-term capital gains (investments held for ≤ 24 months) are added to your income and taxed at slab rates. Long-term capital gains (investments held for > 24 months) are taxed at 20% with indexation benefit. Dividends are taxed at your slab rate, with potential for DTAA credit for foreign taxes paid.

faq.q: Is the 20% TCS an additional tax on global investments?
faq.a: No, the 20% Tax Collected at Source (TCS) on LRS remittances above ₹7 lakh for investments is an advance tax, not an additional tax. It can be claimed as a credit against your total tax liability when filing your Income Tax Return.

faq.q: Can NRIs invest in UCITS ETFs?
faq.a: Yes, Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) can typically invest in UCITS ETFs through international brokerage accounts, often without being subject to the RBI's LRS limits, as LRS applies to resident individuals. However, they need to comply with regulations of their country of residence.
